techniques.label: Surgical Techniques
techniques.title: How We Operate
techniques.description: Three techniques underpin every tumor resection we perform — chosen and combined according to where the tumor sits and what it touches.

items.title: Minimally Invasive Removal
items.text: Micro-neurosurgery and keyhole techniques reach deep-seated tumors through smaller incisions, minimising tissue trauma and shortening recovery.

items.title: Intraoperative Neuronavigation
items.text: A high-resolution computer guidance system — effectively GPS for the brain — tracks tumor boundaries with sub-millimetre precision throughout the operation.

items.title: Awake Brain Mapping
items.text: For tumors near speech or movement centres, the patient stays awake and responsive so those functions can be tested live and protected during resection.

experience.label: Treatment Journey
experience.title: What to Expect, Start to Finish
experience.description: Surgery is one stage in a longer pathway. Here is how care runs from the first scan through to rehabilitation.

items.title: Diagnosis & Imaging
items.text: High-resolution MRI and functional imaging establish the tumor type, its exact boundaries, and which pathways sit closest to it.

items.title: Surgical Planning
items.text: The approach, technique and expected outcome are agreed jointly with neuro-oncology and radiation specialists, then explained to you and your family.

items.title: Micro-Neurosurgery
items.text: Resection under 3D microscopy with live neuronavigation and continuous neuromonitoring, so neural integrity is checked at every stage.

items.title: Recovery & Rehab
items.text: Focused physical, occupational and cognitive therapy to regain strength and coordination, with follow-up medical management throughout.

conditions-we-treat.label: Conditions We Treat
conditions-we-treat.title: Conditions We Treat
conditions-we-treat.description: From nerve compression to structural instability, these are the spinal problems we see and correct most often.

items.title: Herniated & Slip Discs
items.text: Relieving compressed sciatic nerves in the lumbar or cervical spine, restoring pain-free movement and sensation.

items.title: Spinal Canal Stenosis
items.text: Widening narrowed passages in the spinal canal to take pressure off the cord and restore walking capacity.

items.title: Spondylolisthesis
items.text: Stabilising slipped vertebrae using micro-fixation and fusion strategies that preserve as much natural motion as possible.

what-to-expect.label: What to Expect, Start to Finish
what-to-expect.title: What to Expect, Start to Finish
what-to-expect.description: Most spinal problems never reach an operating theatre. Here is the full pathway, from first assessment through rehabilitation.

items.title: Assessment & Imaging
items.text: Clinical examination alongside MRI or CT to identify exactly which structure is compressing which nerve, and how much.

items.title: Conservative Management
items.text: Physiotherapy, targeted injections and medical management are tried first — many patients recover fully without surgery.

items.title: Minimally Invasive Surgery
items.text: Where surgery is needed: laminectomy, microdiscectomy or keyhole fusion through tubular dilators with real-time neural mapping.

items.title: Rehabilitation
items.text: Core mobilisation to safely rebuild lumbar stabilisers, plus posture and ergonomic training to prevent recurring micro-stress on the joints.

vascular-conditions.label: Vascular Conditions Managed
vascular-conditions.title: Vascular Conditions Managed
vascular-conditions.description: Each of these conditions carries a risk of sudden, catastrophic bleeding — which is why they are treated as time-critical.

items.title: Cerebral Aneurysms
items.text: Preventing subarachnoid haemorrhage — bleeding around the brain — by securing the weak point through clipping or coiling.

items.title: Arteriovenous Malformations
items.text: Resecting or embolising complex tangles of arteries and veins before they rupture and bleed into brain tissue.

items.title: Carotid Stenosis
items.text: Carotid endarterectomy or stenting to reopen the narrowed neck arteries that supply the brain, preventing acute stroke.

what-to-expect.label: What to Expect, Start to Finish
what-to-expect.title: What to Expect, Start to Finish
what-to-expect.description: Vascular conditions demand hyper-acute responses. This is how a case moves from presentation to recovery.

items.title: Urgent Imaging
items.text: CT, MRI and angiography establish where the vessel is weak or blocked, and how urgently it needs securing.

items.title: Treatment Planning
items.text: The team decides between open microsurgery and an endovascular approach based on the location, size and shape of the lesion.

items.title: Intervention
items.text: Surgical clipping under the microscope, or micro-catheters fed from the groin for coiling, stent-assisted reconstruction or flow diversion.

items.title: Neuro-ICU & Follow-Up
items.text: Post-operative monitoring in the neuro-ICU to manage vascular spasm and intracranial pressure, then structured outpatient review.

key-indications.label: Key Indications Treated
key-indications.title: Key Indications Treated
key-indications.description: Neuromodulation targets movement disorders where the underlying brain circuit, not the muscle, is the problem.

items.title: DBS for Parkinson's
items.text: Reversing motor fluctuations and the severe medication side-effects that develop in advanced disease, restoring predictable daily function.

items.title: Tremor Control
items.text: Suppressing severe essential tremor so patients can write, eat and hold objects with coordination they had lost.

items.title: Dystonia Relief
items.text: Managing severe, painful muscle spasms by modulating the specific brain circuits driving the abnormal contraction.

what-to-expect.label: What to Expect, Start to Finish
what-to-expect.title: What to Expect, Start to Finish
what-to-expect.description: DBS is a dynamic therapy — the implant is the midpoint of the pathway, not the end of it.

items.title: Candidate Selection
items.text: Detailed movement-disorder assessment establishes whether symptoms are likely to respond to stimulation, and which target is right.

items.title: Stereotactic Planning
items.text: High-resolution imaging maps the precise brain co-ordinates for electrode placement, down to the millimetre.

items.title: Electrode Implantation
items.text: Thin leads are placed in the movement-control regions, connected to a pacemaker-like generator implanted below the collarbone.

items.title: Programming & Support
items.text: Wireless programming sessions tune pulse rate and voltage to the patient’s lifestyle, with caregiver guidance on charging and battery checks.

conditions-we-assess.label: Conditions We Assess
conditions-we-assess.title: Conditions We Assess
conditions-we-assess.description: Dementia affects the entire household, so our care plans cover the family alongside the patient.

items.title: Alzheimer's & Dementia
items.text: Evaluating progressive cognitive decline, memory impairment, spatial disorientation and behavioural change through structured medical strategy.

items.title: Mild Cognitive Impairment
items.text: Addressing early-stage memory change that exceeds normal ageing but does not yet interfere with daily living — the window where intervention matters most.

items.title: Caregiver Support
items.text: Behavioural strategies for confusion, mood change and disturbed sleep-wake cycles, plus home safety guidance to prevent falls and wandering.

what-to-expect.label: What to Expect at Your Assessment
what-to-expect.title: What to Expect at Your Assessment
what-to-expect.description: A full memory assessment is methodical by design — the aim is to find every contributing factor, including the reversible ones.

items.title: Cognitive Testing
items.text: Standardised memory, reasoning and speech assessments (MoCA, MMSE) establish an objective baseline to measure against.

items.title: Advanced Brain Imaging
items.text: High-resolution brain MRI checks for tissue shrinkage, vascular damage and other structural causes of cognitive change.

items.title: Laboratory Panels
items.text: Blood profiles rule out vitamin deficiencies, thyroid imbalance and other treatable contributors to memory loss.

items.title: Care & Caregiver Plan
items.text: A combined plan covering medication, behavioural strategy, home safety and connection to respite services for the family.

key-indications.label: Key Indications Treated
key-indications.title: Key Indications Treated
key-indications.description: rTMS is clinical neuromodulation that targets a variety of chronic, drug-resistant neurological conditions.

items.title: Refractory Depression (TRD)
items.text: Stimulates the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), modulating neural activity to alleviate treatment-resistant mood disorders.

items.title: Stroke Paralysis Recovery
items.text: Encourages neuroplasticity in damaged motor pathways to help patients recover arm/leg movement and coordination post-stroke.

items.title: Chronic Pain & Migraine
items.text: Desensitizes pain pathways in the brain to reduce the frequency and intensity of chronic pain conditions and migraine attacks.

what-to-expect.label: What to Expect During rTMS Treatment
what-to-expect.title: What to Expect During rTMS Treatment
what-to-expect.description: Our protocol ensures patient comfort, clinical mapping accuracy, and tailored treatment parameters.

items.title: Motor Thresholding
items.text: Mapping the patient's motor cortex to identify the exact threshold of stimulation and determine customized dosage guidelines.

items.title: Coil Positioning
items.text: The treatment coil is positioned over the target brain region while the patient rests in a comfortable recliner chair.

items.title: Magnetic Pulses
items.text: Magnetic pulses are delivered in patterns, producing a clicking sound. A tapping feeling on the scalp is felt.

items.title: Immediate Discharge
items.text: Sessions last 20-30 minutes. Once complete, you can drive, work, and resume all activities immediately.

core-therapies.label: Core Rehabilitation Therapies
core-therapies.title: Core Rehabilitation Therapies
core-therapies.description: We combine experienced clinical expertise with state-of-the-art diagnostic and recovery tracking tools to ensure precise treatments.

items.title: Neuro-Physiotherapy
items.text: Focuses on rebuilding muscle strength, improving balance, training gait cycles, and recovering motor control following a stroke, spine injury, or onset of neuropathy.

items.title: Occupational Therapy
items.text: Aids patients in relearning daily living activities (bathing, dressing, writing). We provide cognitive adaptation, motor skills coordination, and assistive technology advice.

items.title: Speech & Swallowing
items.text: Addresses dysphagia (swallowing difficulties) and speech clarity challenges (aphasia/dysarthria) caused by neurological damage, helping patients communicate safely.

recovery-journey.label: Your Recovery Journey
recovery-journey.title: Your Recovery Journey
recovery-journey.description: Our structured recovery protocol ensures patient progress is monitored continuously from admission to outpatient support.

items.title: Baseline Assessment
items.text: Comprehensive clinical evaluation of motor control, cognitive functions, and sensory status to set realistic recovery targets.

items.title: Custom Treatment
items.text: A personalized rehabilitation schedule combining physical therapy, speech pathology, and occupational exercises.

items.title: Active Monitoring
items.text: We utilize advanced biofeedback tools (like Phezee) to monitor joint mobility and electromyography muscle recovery trends in real-time.

items.title: Home Care Care
items.text: Preparing patients for discharge with customized home care guides, training caregivers, and setting up periodic checkups.

types.label: Types of Stroke
types.title: Types of Stroke
types.description: Strokes are divided into categories based on whether they involve blood vessel blockage or rupture.

items.title: Ischemic Stroke
items.text: The most common type (accounts for 87% of strokes). Caused by a blood clot blocking an artery that supplies blood to the brain, cutting off oxygen.

items.title: Hemorrhagic Stroke
items.text: Occurs when a weakened blood vessel ruptures and leaks blood into the surrounding brain tissue, causing severe local pressure and damage.

items.title: Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA)
items.text: Known as a "mini-stroke." Blood flow is blocked temporarily (often resolving within minutes). Although symptoms fade quickly, a TIA is a warning sign of an impending major stroke.

diagnosis.label: How We Diagnose Stroke
diagnosis.title: How We Diagnose Stroke
diagnosis.description: Emergency diagnostics are completed within minutes of arrival to determine if a stroke is ischemic or hemorrhagic, guiding immediate intervention.

items.title: Rapid Neuro Exam
items.text: Immediate clinical checking of sensory inputs, pupillary reflexes, speech clarity, and motor strengths to assess severity.

items.title: Emergency Brain CT
items.text: Fast imaging to rule out brain bleeding (hemorrhage) before prescribing blood thinners or clot-busting medications.

items.title: Brain MRI & MRA
items.text: Detailed imaging scan to trace exact brain tissue damage locations and map arterial blood flow pathways.

items.title: Vascular Ultrasound
items.text: Carotid duplex ultrasound checks for narrow neck arteries or plaques that could spark subsequent strokes.

types.label: Types of Seizures
types.title: Types of Seizures
types.description: Understanding the different types of seizures is crucial for proper diagnosis and treatment. Seizures are categorized based on where they begin in the brain.

items.title: Focal Onset Seizures
items.text: Begin in one area of the brain. May cause changes in sensation, emotions, or movements while the person remains conscious (focal aware) or may cause loss of awareness (focal impaired awareness).

items.title: Generalized Onset Seizures
items.text: Affect both sides of the brain simultaneously from the start. These include absence seizures (brief loss of awareness), tonic seizures (muscle stiffening), and clonic seizures (rhythmic jerking).

items.title: Unknown Onset Seizures
items.text: When the beginning of a seizure cannot be determined as focal or generalized. Further testing and monitoring may be needed to classify the seizure type accurately.

diagnosis.label: How We Diagnose Epilepsy
diagnosis.title: How We Diagnose Epilepsy
diagnosis.description: Accurate diagnosis is the foundation of effective treatment. Our comprehensive diagnostic approach combines clinical evaluation with advanced technology to identify the type and cause of your seizures.

items.title: Clinical Assessment
items.text: Detailed review of your medical history, seizure description, family history, and physical examination to understand your symptoms.

items.title: EEG Monitoring
items.text: Electroencephalogram (EEG) records brain electrical activity to identify seizure patterns and determine the seizure focus.

items.title: Advanced Imaging
items.text: MRI and CT scans to identify structural abnormalities, tumors, or brain lesions that may be causing seizures.

items.title: Lab Tests
items.text: Blood tests and other laboratory investigations to rule out metabolic causes and identify any underlying conditions.

types.label: Common Headache Types
types.title: Common Headache Types
types.description: Headaches are classified as primary (not caused by another condition) or secondary (caused by an underlying health problem).

items.title: Tension Headache
items.text: The most common type, causing a constant dull ache or feeling of tight band pressure around the forehead, back of the head, and neck. Usually related to stress or muscle tension.

items.title: Cluster Headache
items.text: Severe, piercing pain that occurs in cycles or clusters, usually concentrated around one eye. Often accompanied by watering of the eye, nasal congestion, and restlessness.

items.title: Secondary Headache
items.text: Headaches resulting from other medical conditions, such as sinus infections, dental problems, high blood pressure, head injuries, or blood vessel issues in the brain.

diagnosis.label: Diagnosing Headache Disorders
diagnosis.title: Diagnosing Headache Disorders
diagnosis.description: Accurate classification is key. We run dedicated neurological evaluations to differentiate harmless primary headaches from complex secondary conditions.

items.title: Medical History
items.text: In-depth evaluation of your headache patterns, severity, location, duration, family history, and possible lifestyle triggers.

items.title: Neurological Exam
items.text: Testing motor skills, cranial nerve function, sensory responses, balance, and reflexes to verify neurological integrity.

items.title: Brain MRI / CT
items.text: High-resolution imaging to rule out brain abnormalities, aneurysms, tumors, or internal structural issues.

items.title: Lab Tests
items.text: Blood investigations to rule out toxic, endocrine, infectious, or systemic causes behind secondary headache symptoms.

types.label: Types of Migraines
types.title: Types of Migraines
types.description: Migraines are classified depending on the presence of sensory warning signs called auras.

items.title: Migraine with Aura
items.text: Preceded by visual flashes, blind spots, tingling in hands/face, or temporary speech issues about 10-60 minutes before the headache begins.

items.title: Migraine without Aura
items.text: The most common type. Severe, throbbing, one-sided pain occurs without prior warning signs, lasting 4-72 hours if left untreated.

items.title: Chronic Migraine
items.text: Diagnosed when headaches occur on 15 or more days a month for at least 3 months, with at least 8 of those days presenting as typical migraines.

diagnosis.label: Diagnosing Migraines
diagnosis.title: Diagnosing Migraines
diagnosis.description: We combine historical symptom tracking with diagnostic imaging to identify the specific migraine type and formulate a tailored care plan.

items.title: Detailed History
items.text: Mapping pain frequency, location, duration, family history, and associated triggers like stress or diet.

items.title: Neurological Exam
items.text: Checking reflexes, eye movements, sensation, cranial nerve responses, and coordination.

items.title: Brain MRI
items.text: Advanced imaging scans to rule out secondary headache causes, structural issues, or vascular abnormalities.

items.title: Trigger Mapping
items.text: Creating a digital diary tracking lifestyle patterns, hormonal cycles, sleep quality, and diet to narrow triggers.

types.label: Parkinsonian Disorders
types.title: Parkinsonian Disorders
types.description: Symptoms of slowness and tremors can be caused by idiopathic Parkinson's disease or other look-alike syndromes.

items.title: Idiopathic Parkinson's
items.text: The classic form of the disease. Responsive to levodopa therapy. Primary symptoms include resting tremors, muscle stiffness, and slowness.

items.title: Parkinson-Plus
items.text: Syndromes like Multiple System Atrophy (MSA) or Progressive Supranuclear Palsy (PSP) that present with tremors but have additional symptoms and progress differently.

items.title: Drug-Induced
items.text: Reversible parkinsonism symptoms caused by certain medications (such as antipsychotics) that block dopamine receptors in the brain.

diagnosis.label: Diagnosing Parkinson's
diagnosis.title: Diagnosing Parkinson's
diagnosis.description: Diagnosing Parkinson's relies primarily on expert clinical observation of motor patterns, reflexes, and response to specific dopaminergic drugs.

items.title: Clinical Evaluation
items.text: Expert examination of resting tremors, motor rigidity, postural balance, and gait patterns.

items.title: Drug Challenge
items.text: Assessing physical response to Levodopa medication. A significant improvement in motor speed supports a Parkinson's diagnosis.

items.title: DaTscan Imaging
items.text: Dopamine Transporter SPECT scan tracing dopamine pathways in the brain to confirm neurodegenerative drop-offs.

items.title: Brain MRI
items.text: High-resolution imaging scans to rule out atypical parkinsonism, strokes, fluid blockages, or brain stem abnormalities.

types.label: Common Movement Disorders
types.title: Common Movement Disorders
types.description: Movement disorders present as involuntary muscle twitching, steady shaking, or a lack of coordination.

items.title: Essential Tremor
items.text: A common nerve disorder causing involuntary shaking, typically in the hands during active tasks like writing, drinking, or holding objects.

items.title: Dystonia
items.text: Causes involuntary muscle contractions, leading to repetitive twisting movements or abnormal postures (such as writer's cramp or cervical neck twisting).

items.title: Ataxia
items.text: A degenerative condition affecting the cerebellum, resulting in a severe lack of voluntary muscle coordination, balance problems, and unsteady walking.

diagnosis.label: Diagnosing Movement Disorders
diagnosis.title: Diagnosing Movement Disorders
diagnosis.description: Diagnosing movement disorders combines expert motor skill tracking, nerve path conduction tests, and brain scans to map basal ganglia pathways.

items.title: Motor Evaluation
items.text: In-depth testing of reflexes, gait patterns, tremor speed, range of motion, and fine motor skills.

items.title: EMG & Nerve Studies
items.text: Electromyography (EMG) and Nerve Conduction Studies measure electrical pathways inside active muscles and peripheral nerves.

items.title: Brain MRI
items.text: High-resolution imaging scans search for damage in the basal ganglia, cerebellum, or brainstem pathways.

items.title: Genetic Screening
items.text: Investigating chromosomal factors for hereditary conditions like Huntington's disease, ataxia, or early-onset dystonia.

types.label: Types of Multiple Sclerosis
types.title: Types of Multiple Sclerosis
types.description: Multiple Sclerosis manifests differently in each patient, following distinct progression patterns.

items.title: Relapsing-Remitting MS (RRMS)
items.text: The most common form (85% of cases). Defined by clear relapses (attacks) followed by periods of remission where symptoms resolve completely or partially.

items.title: Primary Progressive MS (PPMS)
items.text: Steady worsening of symptoms from the onset without distinct relapses or remissions. Typically diagnosed in patients after age 40.

items.title: Secondary Progressive (SPMS)
items.text: Follows an initial relapsing-remitting course. Over time, the disease transitions into a progressive phase with steady worsening of symptoms between attacks.

diagnosis.label: Diagnosing Multiple Sclerosis
diagnosis.title: Diagnosing Multiple Sclerosis
diagnosis.description: Since there is no single test for MS, diagnosis requires proving "dissemination in time and space"—lesions in different brain areas occurring at different times.

items.title: Clinical Evaluation
items.text: A detailed history of neurological symptoms, relapses, and physical exams tracking sensory and motor nerve deficits.

items.title: Brain & Spine MRI
items.text: High-resolution scans using contrast dye to detect active and scarred lesions (plaques) within myelin structures.

items.title: Lumbar Puncture
items.text: Analyzing spinal fluid to look for oligoclonal bands or specific immunoglobulins indicative of an active CNS immune response.

items.title: Evoked Potentials
items.text: Testing the speed of electrical signals traveling through visual or sensory nerve pathways to detect myelin slowing.

types.label: Neuropathy Categories
types.title: Neuropathy Categories
types.description: Nerve damage is classified by its underlying trigger, guiding our targeted treatment approach.

items.title: Diabetic Neuropathy
items.text: The most common form. High blood sugars over time damage small blood vessels that feed peripheral nerves, resulting in chronic numbness or burning in the feet.

items.title: Inflammatory Neuropathies
items.text: Autoimmune attacks on peripheral myelin. Includes acute Guillain-BarrÃ© Syndrome (GBS) and chronic CIDP, presenting with rapidly progressive muscle weakness.

items.title: Nutritional & Toxic Neuropathy
items.text: Nerve damage due to vitamin deficiencies (such as B12, B1, or B6), chronic alcohol consumption, heavy metals, or chemotherapy drugs.

diagnosis.label: Diagnosing Neuropathy
diagnosis.title: Diagnosing Neuropathy
diagnosis.description: Diagnosing peripheral neuropathy involves checking electrical conduction speed inside nerves, combined with lab screens to pinpoint root causes.

items.title: EMG & NCV Studies
items.text: Nerve Conduction Velocity (NCV) tests and Electromyography (EMG) measure electrical activity in muscles to locate nerve compression or damage.

items.title: Metabolic Lab Tests
items.text: Comprehensive blood screens checking HbA1c (diabetes), vitamin B12 levels, thyroid markers, renal functions, and autoantibodies.

items.title: Quantitative Sensory
items.text: Sensory testing checking temperature shifts, touch thresholds, and vibration limits to identify large vs. small nerve fiber damage.

items.title: Skin Biopsy
items.text: A minimally invasive, 3mm punch skin biopsy to check intraepidermal nerve fiber density, confirming small fiber neuropathy.

types.label: Common Vertigo Types
types.title: Common Vertigo Types
types.description: Vertigo is categorized based on whether the origin is inside the inner ear balance canals or the brain.

items.title: BPPV
items.text: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo. Triggered by specific head movements, caused by tiny calcium carbonate crystals displacing into the inner ear fluid canals.

items.title: Peripheral Vertigo
items.text: Originates in the inner ear balance nerves. Common causes include vestibular neuritis (viral infection of the nerve) and Meniere's disease (fluid build-up in the ear).

items.title: Central Vertigo
items.text: Originates in the brainstem or cerebellum. Triggered by conditions like vestibular migraines, strokes, tumors, or multiple sclerosis.

diagnosis.label: Diagnosing Vertigo
diagnosis.title: Diagnosing Vertigo
diagnosis.description: Diagnosing vertigo involves checking both your balance systems and inner ear fluid pathways to identify positional triggers.

items.title: Dix-Hallpike Maneuver
items.text: A clinical movement test to trigger positional nystagmus (involuntary eye movement) and verify BPPV in the canals.

items.title: Vestibular Testing
items.text: Video-nystagmography (VNG) tests and caloric stimulation check inner ear balance responses.

items.title: Brain MRI
items.text: High-resolution imaging to rule out brainstem strokes, multiple sclerosis plaques, acoustic neuromas, or tumors.

items.title: Hearing Evaluation
items.text: Audiometry screening to rule out Meniere's disease or acoustic nerve issues that affect hearing pathways.
